Answer ALL the SIX questions in this booklet. The mark allocation is indicated for each question. Each question carries 20 marks. In calculations you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. All necessary working must be shown. questions.enonce_markdown:
The half-life of the radioactive isotope lead-210 is 19.7 years.

(i) What is half-life?

(ii) How long will it take for a sample of the isotope to decay to 15% of its original value? *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** The half-life of a radioactive isotope is the **time taken for half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay**, that is, for the amount (and therefore the activity) of the isotope to fall to half of its initial value. It is a constant for a given isotope, independent of the amount present and of temperature or pressure.

**(ii)** Radioactive decay is a first-order process: $N = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}$, with $\lambda = \dfrac{\ln 2}{t_{1/2}}$.

$\lambda = \dfrac{0.693}{19.7\ \text{years}} = 3.52\times10^{-2}\ \text{year}^{-1}$

"Decay to 15 % of its original value" is read as: 15 % of the original amount **remains**, so $N/N_0 = 0.15$.

$t = \dfrac{1}{\lambda}\ln\dfrac{N_0}{N} = \dfrac{19.7}{0.693}\times\ln\dfrac{1}{0.15} = 28.4 \times 1.897 = 53.9\ \text{years}$

**Time $\approx 54$ years** (about 2.7 half-lives: after 2 half-lives 25 % remains, after 3 half-lives 12.5 % remains, which brackets 15 %).

(If the question were read as "15 % has decayed", i.e. 85 % remaining, the time would be $28.4 \times \ln(1/0.85) = 4.6$ years; the usual reading is the one above.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Define order of reaction with respect to a reactant.

(ii) Sketch a graph of rate against concentration of a zero, first and second order reaction on the same grid. *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** The order of reaction with respect to a reactant is the **power to which the concentration of that reactant is raised in the experimentally determined rate equation**; it shows how the rate depends on that concentration. For $\text{rate} = k[\mathrm{A}]^m[\mathrm{B}]^n$, the order with respect to A is $m$ and with respect to B is $n$ (it is found by experiment, not from the stoichiometric equation).

**(ii)** Draw one pair of axes: **rate** (vertical) against **concentration of the reactant, $[\mathrm{A}]$** (horizontal), and label three curves:

| Order | Rate equation | Shape of the rate against $[\mathrm{A}]$ graph |
|---|---|---|
| Zero | $\text{rate} = k$ | a **horizontal straight line** (rate does not depend on $[\mathrm{A}]$), starting at height $k$ on the rate axis |
| First | $\text{rate} = k[\mathrm{A}]$ | a **straight line through the origin**, of gradient $k$ (rate proportional to $[\mathrm{A}]$) |
| Second | $\text{rate} = k[\mathrm{A}]^2$ | a **curve through the origin, concave upwards** (a parabola); the rate quadruples when $[\mathrm{A}]$ doubles |

Key points to show: the three lines are labelled; both axes are labelled; zero order is parallel to the concentration axis; first order is straight through the origin; second order curves upwards, starting below the first-order line at low $[\mathrm{A}]$ and rising above it at high $[\mathrm{A}]$.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Define the following and give a suitable example of each.

(i) Homogeneous catalyst.

(ii) Heterogeneous catalyst. *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Homogeneous catalyst:** a catalyst that is in the **same phase** as the reactants. *Example:* aqueous hydrogen ions, $\mathrm{H^+(aq)}$, catalysing the esterification of ethanol with ethanoic acid (all in the liquid phase); or $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}(aq)}$ catalysing the reaction between $\mathrm{I^-(aq)}$ and $\mathrm{S_2O_8^{2-}(aq)}$.

**(ii) Heterogeneous catalyst:** a catalyst that is in a **different phase** from the reactants (usually a solid catalyst with gaseous or liquid reactants; the reaction occurs on its surface). *Example:* solid iron in the Haber process, $\mathrm{N_2(g)} + 3\mathrm{H_2(g)} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{NH_3(g)}$; or solid vanadium(V) oxide, $\mathrm{V_2O_5(s)}$, in the Contact process; or nickel in the hydrogenation of alkenes.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Define an acid with respect to the Bronsted-Lowry concept.

(ii) Calculate the pH of 0.001 M solution of sulphuric acid. *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** A Bronsted-Lowry acid is a **proton donor** (a species that donates $\mathrm{H^+}$ to a base).

**(ii)** Sulphuric acid is a strong **diprotic** acid; treating both protons as completely ionised:

$\mathrm{H_2SO_4} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{H^+} + \mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}$

$[\mathrm{H^+}] = 2 \times 0.001 = 2.0\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$

$\mathrm{pH} = -\log_{10}[\mathrm{H^+}] = -\log_{10}(2.0\times10^{-3}) = 2.70$

**pH = 2.70.**

(Remark: the second ionisation, $\mathrm{HSO_4^-} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H^+} + \mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}$ with $K_a \approx 1.2\times10^{-2}$, is not quite complete at this dilution; allowing for it gives $[\mathrm{H^+}] \approx 1.87\times10^{-3}$ and pH $\approx 2.73$. The expected answer at this level is 2.70.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
Study the redox systems given and their corresponding standard electrode potentials, then answer the questions that follow.

| | REDOX SYSTEM | $E^\circ$ / volts |
|---|---|---|
| A | $\mathrm{Pb^{2+}} + 2e \longrightarrow \mathrm{Pb(s)}$ | $-0.13$ |
| B | $\mathrm{I_2(aq)} + 2e \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{I^-(aq)}$ | $+0.54$ |
| C | $\mathrm{MnO_4^-(aq)} + 8\mathrm{H^+(aq)} + 5e \longrightarrow \mathrm{Mn^{2+}} + 4\mathrm{H_2O}$ | $+1.51$ |

(i) Identify the strongest oxidizing and reducing agents. Strongest oxidizing agent: ......  Strongest reducing agent: ......

(ii) Write the cell diagram of the cell that results when A and B are coupled and calculate the emf of the cell.

(iii) In which direction will electrons flow in the external circuit when cells A and B are connected? *[5 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** The more positive the $E^\circ$, the stronger the oxidising agent on the left of the half-equation (the species that is reduced); the more negative the $E^\circ$, the stronger the reducing agent, which is the species on the right of the half-equation (the species that is oxidised).

- **Strongest oxidising agent: $\mathrm{MnO_4^-}$** (permanganate ion, system C, $E^\circ = +1.51$ V, the most positive).
- **Strongest reducing agent: $\mathrm{Pb(s)}$** (lead metal, system A, $E^\circ = -0.13$ V, the most negative).

**(ii)** Coupling A and B: system B has the more positive $E^\circ$, so it is the positive electrode (reduction, $\mathrm{I_2} + 2e \rightarrow 2\mathrm{I^-}$); system A is the negative electrode (oxidation, $\mathrm{Pb} \rightarrow \mathrm{Pb^{2+}} + 2e$).

Cell diagram (oxidation on the left, reduction on the right):

$$\mathrm{Pb(s)\ |\ Pb^{2+}(aq)\ ||\ I_2(aq),\ 2I^-(aq)\ |\ Pt(s)}$$

(a platinum electrode is needed in the iodine half-cell because neither $\mathrm{I_2}$ nor $\mathrm{I^-}$ is a solid conductor).

$E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{right}} - E^\circ_{\text{left}} = (+0.54) - (-0.13) = +0.67\ \mathrm{V}$

Overall reaction: $\mathrm{Pb(s)} + \mathrm{I_2(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Pb^{2+}(aq)} + 2\mathrm{I^-(aq)}$, $E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = +0.67$ V (positive, so the reaction is feasible).

**(iii)** Electrons are released at the lead electrode (negative, where oxidation occurs) and flow **through the external circuit (wire) from the lead electrode to the platinum electrode** in the $\mathrm{I_2/I^-}$ half-cell (positive, where reduction occurs), i.e. from A to B.
